$comment: Physically POSSIBLE ranges per property -- not accuracy targets. A value
outside one of these is not 'inaccurate', it is not a value of that quantity
at all, and the usual cause is a unit slip in a generated script.
Why this table exists: a CO2 heat-of-formation run reported -27452 kJ/mol
(experiment: -393.5) because the script pre-converted energies to kJ/mol
before handing them to twain_thermo, which converts again. It was delivered
as 'accepted' -- the plan set target_value and tolerance to null, and no
literature baseline covered the molecule, so nothing in VALIDATE had anything
to compare against. A bound that needs no reference value is the only check
that could have caught it (run 1cd39ffd).
Bounds are deliberately loose -- roughly 2-4x the most extreme real value --
so they can only ever fire on the impossible. That is enough: the smallest
unit slip in play (eV <-> kJ/mol, 96.5x) leaves any real value far outside.
Only properties with a defensible physical bound appear. total_energy and
cohesive_energy are deliberately ABSENT: a total energy's magnitude scales
with electron count and basis set, so no fixed bound distinguishes a unit
error from a bigger molecule.

ranges.reason: a formation enthalpy per mole of formula unit stays within a few thousand kJ/mol
ranges.why: Per mole of formula unit. The most exothermic formations of common species reach a few thousand kJ/mol (large hydrated oxides); C60 sits near +2500. 20000 leaves >4x headroom, while an eV->kJ/mol slip trips it for any |dHf| above 207 kJ/mol -- i.e. essentially every formation enthalpy anyone runs.

ranges.reason: a band gap is non-negative and no known material exceeds ~14 eV
ranges.why: A gap is non-negative by definition (a metal is 0); the widest insulators reach ~14 eV (LiF 14.2). A negative value means the band ordering was read wrong, and an eV->kJ/mol slip exceeds 20 for any gap above 0.2 eV.

ranges.reason: a stable phase has a positive bulk modulus, and diamond -- the stiffest known -- is 443 GPa
ranges.why: Positive for any mechanically stable phase; diamond is 443 GPa and c-BN ~400, so 1000 is over 2x the stiffest known material. Catches a GPa/MPa/Pa slip, which is the common one for an EOS fit.

ranges.reason: logS is a base-10 logarithm of a molar solubility
ranges.why: Already a log, so the bound is tight and safe: -15 is below anything measurable, and +2 would be 100 mol/L, which no solute reaches. Catches a raw concentration reported where a log was asked for.

ranges.reason: osmium, the densest element at ambient conditions, is 22.59 g/cm^3
ranges.why: Positive, and osmium (22.59) is the densest element at ambient conditions. Catches the kg/m^3 slip, a factor of 1000.

ranges.reason: a lattice constant is positive, and even large MOF cells stay well under 100 A
ranges.why: Positive; even large zeolite and MOF cells stay well under 100 A. Catches an A->pm slip (100x) but NOT an A->nm slip (0.1x) -- an upper bound only sees errors in one direction, which is why this table is a backstop and not a substitute for stating units.

ranges.reason: Materials Project's entire distribution lies inside +/-5 eV/atom
ranges.why: Materials Project's whole distribution lies inside +/-5 eV/atom. Catches a per-cell energy reported as per-atom for a large cell, and any eV/kJ confusion.

$comment: Factors tried against an out-of-range value to name the likely cause.
Each is scoped to the units it could possibly apply to: offering
'Hartree -> kJ/mol' as an explanation for a bulk modulus in GPa is
noise, and a wrong hint is worse than none. '*' would mean any unit.
All matching candidates are reported, never a single ranked guess --
loose bounds mean several factors fit, and the check cannot tell which.

factors.label: Hartree -> kJ/mol applied to a value already in kJ/mol
eV -> kJ/mol applied to a value already in kJ/mol
an SI prefix, e.g. GPa read as MPa or kJ as J
